extracted.intended_audience: readers of Samuel Butler's Erewhon / general readers of 19th-century social satire
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from Samuel Butler's Erewhon describing fictional Erewhonian social laws, customs, and reforms (disease policy, punishment, funerary and commemorative practices) used for satirical critique of Victorian institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stern legal repression of diseases
rubrics_metrics.description: “the sternest repression of all diseases whatsoever, as soon as their existence is made manifest to the eye of the law.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the principal remedy to prevent physicians becoming socially/politically powerful; law punishes visible illness promptly to deter its social consequences. Illustrated by the judge’s remarks and the general legal atmosphere that treats disease as an offence requiring public repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility as liability for misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: If you tell me that you had no hand in your parentage and education...I answer that whether your being in a consumption is your fault or no, it is a fault in you, and it is my duty to see that against such faults as this the commonwealth shall be protected. ...I answer that it is your crime to be unfortunate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative judicial principle: misfortune (illness, bad birth) is treated as an individual's fault and as a ground for punishment; justification offered in terms of social protection and responsibility as ‘answerability’ to society. This underpins harsh sentencing and social sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official remedies to be prescribed at conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the most hardened criminal shall be allowed some one of the three official remedies, which is to be prescribed at the time of his conviction. (Judge orders) two tablespoonfuls of castor oil daily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal formality of offering a prescribed physical remedy as the law's merciful provision; in practice remedies are crude and symbolic (e.g., castor oil), and are tied into sentencing rather than therapeutic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory classification of illnesses and mandated treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: He divided all illnesses into three classes—those affecting the head, the trunk, and the lower limbs—and obtained an enactment that all diseases of the head...should be treated with laudanum, those of the body with castor-oil, and those of the lower limbs with an embrocation of strong sulphuric acid and water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top-down, simplistic public-health reform: illnesses are lawfully categorized and assigned single remedies regardless of individual variation. Butler notes practical objections (insufficient care in classification, ill-chosen remedies) but also defends gradual introduction of principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prison labour with deductions for board and conviction costs
rubrics_metrics.description: They would deduct from his earnings the expenses of his board, lodging, surveillance, and half those of his conviction. If he was too ill to do anything for his support in prison, they would allow him nothing but bread and water...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malcontents' proposal for treating diseased prisoners: permit them to work in prison, be minimally provided for, and have earnings largely diverted to cover state expenses—a policy mixing utilitarian economy with minimal welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict surveillance and behavioural restrictions as safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: The loss of liberty, the surveillance, the considerable and compulsory deduction from the prisoner’s earnings, the very sparing use of stimulants (of which they would allow but little to any, and none to those who did not earn them), the enforced celibacy, and above all, the loss of reputation ... are in their opinion as ample safeguards to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-medical controls (surveillance, restriction of stimulants, enforced celibacy, reputational penalties) are explicitly proposed as societal safeguards against spread of illness or neglect of health; these are seen as partial substitutes for harsher physical punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy as justification for humane policy
rubrics_metrics.description: If a course of conduct can be shown to cost a country less...they hold that it requires a good deal to upset the arguments in favour of its being adopted...they think that the more medicinal and humane treatment...would in the long run be much cheaper to the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical, economic argument employed by reformers: humane treatment is advocated on grounds of national cost-saving rather than altruism; appeals to 'men’s pockets' are emphasized as persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging reporting by removing scorn
rubrics_metrics.description: Men will hide their illnesses as long as they are scouted on its becoming known that they are ill...if a man felt that the news of his being in ill-health would be received...they would give themselves up to the police as readily on perceiving that they had taken small-pox, as they go now to the straightener when they feel that they are on the point of forging a will...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social policy principle: reduce stigmatization and punitive shame to encourage self-reporting and early treatment; the current scorn is blamed for concealment and worse public health outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cremation and scattering of ashes at chosen locality
rubrics_metrics.description: They burn their dead, and the ashes are presently scattered over any piece of ground which the deceased may himself have chosen. No one is permitted to refuse this hospitality to the dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funerary custom: mandatory cremation with ashes dispersed on personally chosen land; social belief that ashes make the land's jealous guardians—practice replaces monuments and epitaphs as means of associating the dead with place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statues of living persons instead of posthumous monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: They have statues of themselves made while they are still alive (those, that is, who can afford it), and write inscriptions under them...If a person is ugly he does not sit as a model for his own statue, although it bears his name. He gets the handsomest of his friends to sit for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom encourages self-commemoration in life; inscriptions tend to be untruthful in a different way from epitaphs; social etiquette (women sit for their own statues; idealisation expected) and perverse incentives (friends posing for ugly sitters) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statue regulation: fifty-year life and jury reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: An Act to the effect that no statue of any public man or woman should be allowed to remain unbroken for more than fifty years, unless at the end of that time a jury of twenty-four men taken at random from the street pronounced in favour of its being allowed a second fifty years of life. Every fifty years this reconsideration was to be repeated, and unless there was a majority of eighteen in favour of the retention of the statue, it was to be destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative mechanism to prevent proliferation and permanence of public statues; produces deterrent effects (fewer commissions) and perverse adaptations (commissions paid to not make a statue). Suggested as a pragmatic solution to statue clutter and artistic decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative proposal: forbid statues until 100 years after death
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps a simpler plan would have been to forbid the erection of a statue to any public man or woman till he or she had been dead at least one hundred years, and even then to insist on reconsideration of the claims of the deceased and the merit of the statue every fifty years...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial suggestion / legislative alternative aimed at reducing frivolous or short-lived commemoration; presented as possibly simpler though the working Act is judged satisfactory overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiquette of condolence: boxes of artificial tears with specified counts
rubrics_metrics.description: When any one dies, the friends of the family write no letters of condolence, neither do they attend the scattering, nor wear mourning, but they send little boxes filled with artificial tears, and with the name of the sender painted neatly upon the outside of the lid. The tears vary in number from two to fifteen or sixteen, according to degree of intimacy or relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly codified, quantized etiquette: number of tears signals degree of intimacy; customs have evolved (tears once stuck to cheeks, then worn on hat, now no longer worn). Omission of an expected number is socially felt; this replaces written condolences and public mourning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of births; birth-formula and social penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The birth of a child is looked upon as a painful subject on which it is kinder not to touch: the illness of the mother is carefully concealed until the necessity for signing the birth-formula...When the offence is over and done with, it is condoned...the baby is kept out of sight, except on the day of signing the birth-formula, until it can walk and talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong social pressure to hide childbirth and maternal illness; formal 'birth-formula' triggers disclosure; public condemnation follows conspicuous births, and a coroner’s inquest on infant death leads to widespread falsification (e.g., claiming the child was 'over seventy-five years old') to avoid disgrace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycle of artistic rise, decline, and statutory controls
rubrics_metrics.description: All the noblest arts hold in perfection but for a very little moment...At last the evil reached such a pitch that the people rose, and with indiscriminate fury destroyed good and bad alike. ...for a couple of hundred years or so, not a statue was made from one end of the kingdom to the other, but...earliest sculptors of this period...again produced works that were full of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive cultural principle: artistic practices tend to peak and then degenerate into trade and bad copying, provoking iconoclastic reactions and legal or popular restraints; policy responses (statutory limits) aim to correct cycles but also produce side effects (suppression then revival).
